scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Logobi appeared in the 1980s in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, specifically within popular neighborhoods like Abobo.
It was developed by street gang members, with John Pololo recognized as the primary figure who codified the dance by mixing martial arts gestures with music.

narration: The dance conveys the social realities of poverty and misery while aspiring toward a more positive future, justice, and peace.
It serves as a medium for youth to express their identity and navigate the challenges of urban life.

narration: The dance is characterized by rapid, expressive arm movements and jerky footwork.

The style relies heavily on individual improvisation and high-energy execution.

narration: Historically performed in the ghettos and maquis of Abidjan, the dance moved to public spaces in France, including metro stations, train stations, and shopping malls, where it was performed in street battles.

scenes.title: The people
narration: John Pololo (Sahiri Gnédré Lazare) is the seminal figure.
Other associated artists include Moussier Tombola, Les Youlés, Samo Samo, Petit Denis, and Gor la Montagne.

The Ivorian version remains closer to its 'loubard' roots and Zouglou origins, while the French version is a hybrid incorporating tecktonik and electronic music, often geared toward a younger, broader audience.
Logobi is a descendant of Zouglou and a precursor to the coupé-décalé movement.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: logobi is parent of Zouglou: Logobi evolved from Zouglou, adopting its rhythmic base while developing a more aggressive, street-focused identity.
logobi is influence of Coupé-décalé: Logobi influenced the development of coupé-décalé and often shares its musical instrumentals.
